items.title: Why I Put my Failures on Sticky Notes?
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
Next to my computer screen, it is filled with sticky notes with names on it. Those are the customers that I have lost or mistakes that I made which resulted in massive losses. I am not a smart person; I can only brute force myself to success. Thus, I need to outwork everyone else in the market.

It is uncomfortable to be reminded of my failure. Each name has its own painful lesson. I vow not to make those mistakes. Therefore, I have to see those names every day. Is it miserable? Yes. In fact, it is very miserable. It is only through misery that we can learn the lesson.

This year, I have accumulated more losses than I want to remember. It is difficult to stay positive and stay on the path. But I must try and keep moving.

items.title: Emergence and centralised planning of scientific research
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

 Scientists, individually and collectively, make decisions about research directions and priorities. There are three main interacting influences on these decisions: the individual scientists, the scientific community they are part of, and the broader context (social, political, and economic). The latter drives funding decisions and career incentives. Over the past few decades, the latter influences have grown much stronger. For example, there is a greater emphasis on volume of output, quantity of funding, economic benefits, short-term technological outcomes, large collaborations, publicity, management of projects according to tight timelines, metrics, and publication in luxury journals. We are a long way from the curiosity-driven research of individual investigators. In other words, research decisions are now largely "top down" rather than "bottom up." Managers at funding agencies and universities have inordinate influence.

items.title: MPS
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
Subject: The stop-reading method, with a finger as your eye tracker

Team,

Several of you asked how to finish a question in about 90 seconds. The method below rests on one rule: stop reading once you can answer. You do not need lab equipment to test whether you follow it. Point at the screen or page where your attention settles, and have a partner watch.

A finger-pointing check

Eye tracking records fixations (pauses where the eyes hold still) and saccades (the quick jumps between them). We did not record eye movements during these sessions, so what follows is a working model, not measured data.

You can run a cheaper version. Point at the word or line you are reading, and keep your finger there while you think. A partner watches and marks each place your finger returns to. Pointing is slower than gaze, so it shows where your attention settles, not every glance. That is enough to spot the habits that cost time: looping back to the top of the stem, lingering on a distractor, or…

items.title: Where we’re going, we don’t need chatbots
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
“You’ve been working hard, why not take a weekend vacation!”

Your chatbot says, after a 72 hour unattended session. It says that New York is nice this time of year. You ask it to book the cheapest flights. Half the airlines respond with a 429 code because your residential IP is part of five botnets. That’s odd you think, you only signed up to two that you can remember.

items.title: 💬 Snippet!
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
What happens when words disappear, when they escape and run away? 

When I write of darkness; a wish to share, to tell you —you are not alone, I was there too.  

Yet the words shout —No! —and off they go, packed up their bags, dragged them over the floor; for it was heavy, heavy baggage of my heart, off they go. 

Where do they go, that rebellious testimony of my humanity, witness of suffering, flickering of the light? Where do they hide? It seems the ink had not dried.

Why do some words run away and others stay? 

I guess I should be grateful, for he will never gaze at the darkness of that dream. 

#100words_100days #poetry #words

I'm looking for resources or advice to get over abandonment issues, specifically from a biological father who was never there.

My biological dad has never been in my life. I have a few fleeting early-childhood memories of him coming over to my house, having sex with my mom, completely ignoring me, and leaving. Other than that I have never seen or met this man.

When I was around 5-6 my mom married my step-dad, who for all intents and purposes I consider to be my dad. Then he died when I was in my mid-20s. I'm resentful that the guy who chose to raise me got cancer and died, while the guy who never wanted to be in my life is still alive and well.

Recently, it's been revealed that my mom still occasionally sees my biological dad. Whenever I mention that this makes me feel bad, she kind of brushes it off and ignores it, which has negatively impacted my relationship with her.
